- OS: Windows
- hk: since commit a810c3b (#1194, merged)
- Affected builtins: any migrated to argv that resolve to a `node_modules/.bin` shim (oxlint, eslint, ...)
- Not affected: Linux; Windows with a globally-installed `.exe`

## Reproduction

1. On Windows, in a repo with `oxlint` (or `eslint`) installed as an npm dev dependency (so `node_modules/.bin/oxlint.cmd` exists).
2. Run `hk run check` (or trigger the `ox_lint` / `eslint` step).
3. The step fails reporting the executable cannot be found.

## Root cause

#1194 switched ~100 builtins from shell-string commands to structured `Config.Command { argv = [...] }`. The two command forms take different execution paths in `src/step/runner.rs`:

- **Shell form** (before #1194) renders to a single string and, on Windows with the default `Cmd` shell, runs via `cmd.exe /c <rendered>` (`runner.rs:296`). `cmd.exe` resolves the executable using `PATHEXT` (`.COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD;...`), so the bare name `oxlint` matches `node_modules/.bin/oxlint.cmd`.

- **Argv form** (after #1194) runs via `CmdLineRunner::new_direct(&argv[0])` (`runner.rs:276`), which calls Rust's `std::process::Command::new("oxlint")` directly, bypassing `cmd.exe` entirely (see `ensembler/src/cmd.rs`, `new_direct`).

Per the Rust std docs for [`Command` on Windows](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Command.html#searching):

> For executable files, the `.exe` extension may be omitted. Files with other extensions must include the extension, otherwise they will not be found.

`CreateProcessW` (the Win32 API Rust uses) only appends `.exe`; it does **not** consult `PATHEXT`. npm shims under `node_modules/.bin/` are `oxlint` (extensionless shell script) and `oxlint.cmd` — neither is a `.exe`, so `Command::new("oxlint")` cannot find them.

On Linux, `new_direct` falls back to `execvp`, which searches `PATH` and happily executes the extensionless shim (it has the executable bit), so the same argv form works.

## Why only `node_modules` installs are affected

Global installs (mise, cargo, scoop, ...) provide a real `oxlint.exe`, which `CreateProcessW` resolves via the implicit `.exe` append. `node_modules/.bin/` only provides `.cmd`/extensionless shims, which `CreateProcessW` cannot resolve without `PATHEXT`.

- `pkl/builtins/ox_lint.pkl` — argv form introduced by #1194
- `src/step/runner.rs:276` — `RenderedCommand::Argv(argv) => CmdLineRunner::new_direct(&argv[0]).args(&argv[1..])`
- `src/step/runner.rs:296` — shell form on Windows: `CmdLineRunner::new_direct("cmd.exe").arg("/c").raw_arg(run)`
- `ensembler/src/cmd.rs` — `new()` wraps `cmd.exe /c` on Windows; `new_direct()` does not

The feature code is correct, but **every released binary ships an empty embedded package**, so it's a silent no-op — `hk validate` (and anything that evaluates `hk.pkl`) still needs the network.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reproduction\\r\\n\\r\\nWith hk 1.57.0 from the release, a config pinning the running version, a cold cache, and offline mode:\\r\\n\\r\\n```console\\r\\n$ cat hk.pkl\\r\\namends \\\"package://github.com/jdx/hk/releases/download/v1.57.0/hk@1.57.0#/Config.pkl\\\"\\r\\nhooks { [\\\"check\\\"] { steps { [\\\"echo\\\"] { check = \\\"echo ok\\\" } } } }\\r\\n\\r\\n$ HK_PKL_CACHE_DIR=$(mktemp -d) HK_PKL_OFFLINE=1 hk validate\\r\\nEval error: package is not cached and offline mode is enabled:\\r\\n  https://github.com/jdx/hk/releases/download/v1.57.0/hk@1.57.0.zip\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIt behaves identically for a matching version and a bogus one (e.g. `0.0.0`), which is the tell that the embedded bytes are empty. Building locally (which runs `pkl:gen` first) embeds a real ~100 KB zip and the same config then validates offline on a cold cache; setting `HK_PKL_EMBEDDED=0` makes it fail again — confirming the embed is what does the work.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Root cause\\r\\n\\r\\n`build/embed_pkl_package.rs` requires `Builtins.pkl` (in `REQUIRED_MODULES`) and writes an empty placeholder if any required module is missing. `pkl/Builtins.pkl` is `.gitignore`d — it's generated by `pkl:gen`, not committed.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe release `build-binaries` job never generates it:\\r\\n\\r\\n- optimized targets → `scripts/pgo-bolt.bash` → `cargo`/`cross build` directly\\r\\n- other targets → `taiki-e/upload-rust-binary-action` → `cargo`/`cross build` directly\\r\\n\\r\\n`pkl:gen` only runs as a dependency of the mise build/test tasks (`build`, `test:cargo`, `pkl:dist`, `docs:gen`, …). The release job bypasses all of them and invokes `cargo`/`cross build` directly, so `pkl:gen` never runs. At `build.rs` time `pkl/Builtins.pkl` is therefore absent → empty zip → `EMBEDDED_PKL_PACKAGE.is_empty()` → preload skipped.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe bats tests in `test/pkl_embedded_package.bats` pass because `ci-impl.yml` runs `pkl:gen` before them, so the gap is release-only and the suite doesn't catch it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Suggested fix\\r\\n\\r\\nRun `pkl:gen` before the build in the `build-binaries` job so `pkl/Builtins.pkl` exists when `build.rs` runs. The job currently sets up no mise/python, so it needs a mise setup step first (mirroring `ci-impl.yml`). A single insertion after checkout covers both build paths (the optimized `pgo-bolt.bash` and `upload-rust-binary-action`):\\r\\n\\r\\n```diff\\r\\n       - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1\\r\\n         with:\\r\\n           persist-credentials: false\\r\\n+      - uses: jdx/mise-action@3c2e0cf82a5b2e5249f0d3635a4d83d0ae861518 # v4.2.5\\r\\n+        with:\\r\\n+          cache: false\\r\\n+      # Generate pkl/Builtins.pkl so build.rs embeds a non-empty package.\\r\\n+      # No shell: override — mise selects gen.ps1 on Windows, gen on *nix.\\r\\n+      - name: Generate pkl builtins for the embedded package\\r\\n+        run: mise run pkl:gen\\r\\n       - if: matrix.os == 'macos-latest'\\r\\n         uses: apple-actions/import-codesign-certs@5142e029c445c10ffc7149d172e540235a065466 # v7\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo things to watch:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Windows.** The bash `pkl:gen` task early-exits on Windows; the PowerShell variant `mise-tasks/pkl/gen.ps1` handles it. So the step must not force `shell: bash`, or the Windows release binaries would still ship an empty embed — let mise pick the per-platform task.\\r\\n- **`cross` targets.** `pkl:gen` runs on the host runner; `cross` mounts the workspace, so the generated file is present when `build.rs` runs in the container.\\r\\n\\r\\nOptionally, harden `embed_pkl_package.rs` so a missing-source build fails loudly instead of silently embedding an empty zip and falling back to the network — e.g. gate the empty-file branch on a release flag:\\r\\n\\r\\n```rust\\r\\nif !complete {\\r\\n    if std::env::var_os(\\\"HK_REQUIRE_EMBEDDED_PKL\\\").is_some() {\\r\\n        return Err(std::io::Error::other(\\\"pkl sources missing; run pkl:gen\\\"));\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    fs::write(&dest_path, b\\\"\\\")?;\\r\\n    return Ok(());\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nwith that env var set in the release job. The CI step alone fixes the bug; this just keeps it from regressing unnoticed.\\r\\n\",\"comments\":{\"nodes\":[{\"author\":{\"login\":\"sahidvelji\"},\"body\":\"Working on a PR for this now, so no need for anyone else to pick it up.\\n\\nIt takes the suggested fix (mise setup + `pkl:gen` before the build in `build-binaries`) plus the optional hardening (`HK_REQUIRE_EMBEDDED_PKL` turning a missing-source build into a hard error), with two details the writeup missed:\\n\\n- `mise install` brings in mr-boxington, whose postinstall points plain `cargo` at the mbx shim. Release binaries are built by `cargo`/`cross` directly today, so the job pins `MBX_DISABLE=1` to keep that unchanged.\\n- `cross` filters host env at the container boundary, so `HK_REQUIRE_EMBEDDED_PKL` needs a `passthrough` entry in `Cross.toml` or the guard would be a no-op on the four cross targets — the same silent failure mode.\\n\\n*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-5; version: 2.1.236.*\",\"replies\":{\"nodes\":[]}}]}},{\"number\":1296,\"title\":\"[Docs] Lefthook described inaccurately in comparisons\",\"url\":\"https://github.com/jdx/hk/discussions/1296\",\"body\":\"https://hk.jdx.dev/why-hk.html says lots of times that Lefthook does no stash management whatsoever.  This seems to be incorrect; it has done some since 1.3.0, although there are several open issues about it (eg. evilmartians/lefthook#833, evilmartians/lefthook#1480) so it might not do it *well*.\\r\\n\\r\\nI havenʼt personally used it (Iʼm looking at hk because Iʼm trying to find a hook manager), so it might just do nothing, but some of those issues seem like they couldnʼt exist if it werenʼt even trying to stash unstaged changes.\",\"comments\":{\"nodes\":[{\"author\":{\"login\":\"jdx\"},\"body\":\"Thanks for the correction—you’re right. Lefthook has hidden and restored tracked, partially staged changes for pre-…507 tokens truncated…l` configs against the current builtins, three concrete builtin improvements fell out. Each one lets a downstream config drop a hand-written override or a fully hand-rolled step. They're independent — feel free to split into separate issues/PRs — but they share the same provenance so I'm filing them together.\\n\\nSummary:\\n\\n1. **`gomod_tidy`** — broaden the glob so `go mod tidy` actually runs when `.go` imports change, not only when `go.mod` itself is edited.\\n2. **`shellcheck`** — add a `fix` (the builtin is check-only today; shellcheck can autofix a subset via its diff output).\\n3. **New `ls_lint` builtin** — there's no builtin for ls-lint (directory/filename naming), so users hand-roll the whole step.\\n\\nEach proposal below is self-contained: motivation, exact file/code, tests, verification, and caveats.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Proposal 1 — broaden `gomod_tidy`'s glob\\n\\n### Motivation\\n\\n`go mod tidy` adds missing and removes unused module requirements based on the **imports in `.go` files**. The current builtin only triggers when `go.mod` itself changes:\\n\\n```pkl\\n// pkl/builtins/gomod_tidy.pkl (current)\\ngomod_tidy = new Config.Step {\\n  glob = \\\"**/go.mod\\\"\\n  workspace_indicator = \\\"go.mod\\\"\\n  dir = \\\"{{workspace}}\\\"\\n  ...\\n```\\n\\nSo the most common drift — you add or remove an `import` in a `.go` file and `go.mod`/`go.sum` are now out of tidy — is **not caught at commit time**, because editing a `.go` file doesn't match `**/go.mod`. A real-world config worked around this by overriding the glob to `List(\\\"**/*.go\\\", \\\"go.mod\\\", \\\"go.sum\\\")`.\\n\\n### Proposed change\\n\\nChange the glob to include `.go` files and `go.sum` (single line in `pkl/builtins/gomod_tidy.pkl`):\\n\\n```pkl\\ngomod_tidy = new Config.Step {\\n  glob = List(\\\"**/*.go\\\", \\\"**/go.mod\\\", \\\"**/go.sum\\\")\\n  workspace_indicator = \\\"go.mod\\\"\\n  dir = \\\"{{workspace}}\\\"\\n  ...\\n```\\n\\nEverything else stays the same. `workspace_indicator = \\\"go.mod\\\"` + `dir = \\\"{{workspace}}\\\"` still resolve the correct module directory, and the command still ignores `{{files}}` (it runs `go mod tidy [-diff]` in the workspace).\\n\\n### Trade-off to weigh\\n\\nThis makes the step run `go mod tidy -diff` whenever any Go file changes rather than only on `go.mod` edits. In check mode `-diff` is cheap, and it's the correct scope — but it does run more often. If that's a concern, an alternative is to keep `**/go.mod` as-is and document the broader glob as the recommended override. My recommendation is to broaden it in the builtin, since the narrow glob silently misses the primary use case.\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\nThe existing tests in `gomod_tidy.pkl` all write `go.mod` + `main.go` and should continue to pass unchanged (both match the broadened glob). A `.go`-driven \\\"tidy adds a missing require\\\" test would need network access to resolve a real module, so it isn't suitable for the offline pkl test sandbox — the existing \\\"remove unused require\\\" fix test already covers the tidy path. No test changes are strictly required; add a comment on the glob explaining why `.go`/`go.sum` are included.\\n\\n### Verification\\n\\n```bash\\nmise run pkl:gen            # regenerate the aggregated Builtins.pkl\\nhk test --step gomod_tidy   # all existing tests should pass\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Proposal 2 — add a `fix` to the `shellcheck` builtin\\n\\n### Motivation\\n\\nThe `shellcheck` builtin (`pkl/builtins/shellcheck.pkl`) defines only `check` — there's no `fix`. shellcheck has no in-place write mode, but it can emit a unified diff of the fixes it's able to make (`--format=diff`), which can be applied with `git apply`. A real-world config added exactly this:\\n\\n```pkl\\nfix = \\\"shellcheck --norc -f diff {{files}} | git apply --allow-empty\\\"\\n```\\n\\nAdding a `fix` to the builtin removes the need for that override and gives `hk fix` a partial shellcheck autofixer for free.\\n\\n### Behavior I verified (shellcheck 0.11.0, in a git repo)\\n\\nAgainst a script with an autofixable finding (`x=\\\\`date\\\\`` → `x=$(date)`, SC2006):\\n\\n- **Autofixable finding:** `shellcheck --format=diff file.sh` prints a unified diff to **stdout** and exits **1**. Run with a relative path **inside a git repo, shellcheck emits git-style `a/`…`b/…` diff headers** (verified — see the `git apply` note below), so `git apply` applies it at its default strip level.\\n- **Only non-autofixable findings:** the message `Issues were detected, but none were auto-fixable...` goes to **stderr** (not stdout), stdout is empty, exit **1**.\\n- **Clean file:** empty stdout, exit **0**.\\n\\nBecause the \\\"none were auto-fixable\\\" note is on stderr, piping stdout to `git apply` only ever feeds it a real diff or nothing, and `--allow-empty` handles the nothing case. In a pipeline the exit code is `git apply`'s, so the fix step exits 0 when it applies (or has nothing to apply); any remaining non-autofixable findings are still reported by `check`. This is the same \\\"fix what you can, check flags the rest\\\" model as `eslint --fix`.\\n\\n### Proposed change\\n\\nAdd a `fix` to `pkl/builtins/shellcheck.pkl`. The existing `check` uses the `argv` form; the fix needs a shell pipeline, so it must use the shell-string form of `CommandSpec`:\\n\\n```pkl\\nshellcheck = new Config.Step {\\n  batch = true\\n  match_any =\\n    List(\\n      new Config.FileSelector { glob = List(\\\"**/*.sh\\\", \\\"**/*.bash\\\") },\\n      new Config.FileSelector { types = List(\\\"sh\\\", \\\"bash\\\") },\\n    )\\n  check = new Config.CommandSpec {\\n    command = new Config.Command { argv = List(\\\"shellcheck\\\", \\\"{{files}}\\\") }\\n    effect = \\\"read\\\"\\n  }\\n  // shellcheck has no in-place write mode; the only autofix path is its unified\\n  // diff applied with git apply. Only a subset of findings are auto-fixable\\n  // (e.g. SC2006 backticks -> $()); the rest remain reported by `check`. The\\n  // \\\"none were auto-fixable\\\" note goes to stderr, so stdout is either a clean\\n  // diff or empty -- `--allow-empty` covers the empty case.\\n  fix = new Config.CommandSpec {\\n    command = \\\"shellcheck --format=diff {{files}} | git apply --allow-empty\\\"\\n    effect = \\\"write\\\"\\n  }\\n  tests { ... }   // see below\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### `git apply` strip level — verified, use the default (`-p1`)\\n\\nI confirmed this end-to-end (shellcheck 0.11.0, git 2.x): when shellcheck is given a **relative** path from within a git repo, its diff headers use the git-style `a/…` `b/…` prefixes:\\n\\n```\\n--- a/t.sh\\n+++ b/t.sh\\n```\\n\\nSo plain `git apply --allow-empty` (default `-p1`) applies cleanly, and `git apply -p0` **fails** with `error: b/t.sh: No such file or directory`. Since hk runs steps from the repo root with repo-relative `{{files}}`, this is the correct and tested form — **do not add `-p0`**. (An earlier ad-hoc test that passed an *absolute* path produced prefix-less headers; that case doesn't apply to how hk invokes steps, but it's why the fix tests below matter as a guard.)\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\n`git apply` needs a git working tree, so the fix tests must init one via `TestMaker.before`. Add to the `tests` block (the `helpers.TestMaker` supports a `before` field, used the same way `actionlint`/`no_commit_to_branch` do):\\n\\n```pkl\\n// existing check tests stay as-is\\nlocal const fixMaker = new helpers.TestMaker {\\n  filename = \\\"test.sh\\\"\\n  before = \\\"git init -q\\\"\\n}\\n// SC2006: backticks are auto-fixable to $()\\nlocal const backtickBad = \\\"#!/bin/sh\\\\nx=`date`\\\\necho \\\\\\\"$x\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\"\\nlocal const backtickGood = \\\"#!/bin/sh\\\\nx=$(date)\\\\necho \\\\\\\"$x\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\"\\n[\\\"fix autofixable file\\\"] = fixMaker.fixPass(backtickBad, backtickGood)\\n[\\\"fix clean file\\\"] = fixMaker.fixPass(backtickGood, backtickGood)\\n```\\n\\nConsider also a test where the file has only a non-autofixable finding (e.g. an unquoted `$var`, SC2086) and asserting `fix` leaves it unchanged and exits 0 (nothing to apply) while `check` still fails — this documents the partial-fix contract.\\n\\n### Verification\\n\\n```bash\\nmise run pkl:gen\\nhk test --step shellcheck\\n```\\n\\nThe `fix autofixable file` test is the guard for the strip-level detail above; it must pass with the plain `git apply --allow-empty` command.\\n\\n### Caveats to note in the PR\\n\\n- Requires `git` on PATH — always true for hk (it's a git hook manager), and the fix tests init a repo.\\n- Only a subset of shellcheck findings are auto-fixable; this is a partial fixer by design.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Proposal 3 — new `ls_lint` builtin\\n\\n### Motivation\\n\\n[ls-lint](https://ls-lint.org) enforces directory and filename naming conventions. There's no builtin for it today, so users hand-roll the entire step. A real-world config has:\\n\\n```pkl\\n[\\\"ls-lint\\\"] {\\n  glob = \\\"**/*.go\\\"\\n  check = \\\"ls-lint -config .config/.ls-lint.yml\\\"\\n}\\n```\\n\\nA builtin would provide the tool install, the right command/effect, and project indicators.\\n\\n### Proposed builtin\\n\\nNew file `pkl/builtins/ls_lint.pkl`:\\n\\n```pkl\\nimport \\\"../Builtins.pkl\\\"\\nimport \\\"../Config.pkl\\\"\\nimport \\\"./test/helpers.pkl\\\"\\n\\n@Builtins.meta {\\n  category = \\\"Special Purpose\\\"\\n  description = \\\"Directory and filename naming linter\\\"\\n  project_indicators {\\n    new { file = \\\".ls-lint.yml\\\" }\\n    new { file = \\\".ls-lint.yaml\\\" }\\n  }\\n}\\nls_lint = new Config.Step {\\n  // ls-lint validates the whole tree against .ls-lint.yml and takes no file\\n  // arguments (usage: `ls-lint [options] [file|dir]*`, defaults to \\\".\\\"), so it\\n  // runs once per invocation (batch=false, no {{files}}). The glob only gates\\n  // whether the step runs when files change.\\n  glob = \\\"**/*\\\"\\n  batch = false\\n  check = new Config.CommandSpec {\\n    command = new Config.Command { argv = List(\\\"ls-lint\\\") }\\n    effect = \\\"read\\\"\\n  }\\n  // ls-lint intentionally has no fix: it will not rename files for you.\\n  tests { ... }   // see below\\n}\\n```\\n\\nModeling note: this follows the same shape as the `mise` builtin (a tool that scans everything itself and takes no file args → `batch = false`, no `{{files}}`). Confirm during implementation that this runs `ls-lint` exactly once when multiple files change; if batching still causes multiple invocations, drop the `glob` entirely so it runs once per hook invocation (the `no_commit_to_branch` pattern). ls-lint also has a `-workdir <dir>` flag if a workspace-scoped variant is ever wanted.\\n\\n### Tool stub\\n\\nAdd `test/builtin_tool_stubs/ls-lint` (mirrors the other stubs):\\n\\n```\\n#!/usr/bin/env -S mise tool-stub\\n\\nversion = \\\"2\\\"\\ntool = \\\"aqua:loeffel-io/ls-lint\\\"\\n```\\n\\nVerified: `aqua:loeffel-io/ls-lint@2` resolves to `2.3.1` via aqua and installs cleanly.\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\nls-lint checks **filenames**, not contents, so the tests vary the filename and ship an `.ls-lint.yml`. I verified the config syntax, flag, and exit codes with ls-lint **v2.3.1**:\\n\\n- Config `ls:\\\\n  .go: snake_case\\\\n` at the repo root is auto-discovered.\\n- A snake-case-violating name (`BadName.go`) → exit **1** (`BadName.go failed for `.go` rules: snakecase`); a compliant name (`good_name.go`) → exit **0**.\\n- The config flag is `-config <path>` (single dash, as shown in `--help`); `--config` is also accepted.\\n\\n```pkl\\nlocal const config = \\\"ls:\\\\n  .go: snake_case\\\\n\\\"\\nlocal const badMaker = new helpers.TestMaker {\\n  filename = \\\"BadName.go\\\"\\n  extra_files = new Mapping<String, String> { [\\\".ls-lint.yml\\\"] = config }\\n}\\nlocal const goodMaker = new helpers.TestMaker {\\n  filename = \\\"good_name.go\\\"\\n  extra_files = new Mapping<String, String> { [\\\".ls-lint.yml\\\"] = config }\\n}\\n[\\\"check bad filename\\\"] = badMaker.checkFail(\\\"package x\\\\n\\\", 1)\\n[\\\"check good filename\\\"] = goodMaker.checkPass(\\\"package x\\\\n\\\")\\n```\\n\\n(`import \\\"./test/helpers.pkl\\\"` is already included in the file above.)\\n\\n### Does this let a config drop its override? Partially — worth stating in the docs\\n\\nA downstream config can use `Builtins.ls_lint` directly **only if its config lives at the repo root** as `.ls-lint.yml`/`.ls-lint.yaml`. I confirmed ls-lint does **not** search `.config/`: with the config only at `.config/.ls-lint.yml` and no flag, ls-lint errors `open .ls-lint.yml: no such file or directory` and exits 1. A config that keeps `.config/.ls-lint.yml` will still need to override `check` to pass `-config .config/.ls-lint.yml` (or relocate the file to the root). Same situation as `ryl`/`yamlfmt` with non-standard config paths — `project_indicators` gate auto-enable but don't pass `-config` to the tool. The builtin still removes most of the boilerplate (tool install, effect, indicators) either way.\\n\\n### Verification\\n\\n```bash\\nmise use -g \\\"aqua:loeffel-io/ls-lint@2\\\"   # resolves to 2.3.1\\nmise run pkl:gen                            # picks up the new builtin via import*\\nhk test --step ls_lint\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Implementation notes for whoever picks this up\\n\\n- **Regeneration is required for all three.** `pkl/Builtins.pkl` is a generated aggregate (not committed as source in the usual sense) built from `pkl/builtins/*.pkl` via `scripts/gen_builtins.py`, run with `mise run pkl:gen`. It uses `import* \\\"builtins/*.pkl\\\"`, so a new file like `ls_lint.pkl` is auto-discovered and exposed as `Builtins.ls_lint`. Run `mise run pkl:gen` after any builtin change and check `git status` for what to commit.\\n- **Docs:** regenerate builtin docs if the repo tracks them (`mise run docs:gen` / see `bin/generate_docs.rs`) and commit the result.\\n- **Run the builtin tests** for each changed/added step: `hk test --step <name>`, plus `mise run test:bats test/builtins_tests.bats` to exercise them the way CI does.\\n- **Conventional commits / scope `builtins`**, e.g.:\\n  - `fix(builtins): broaden gomod_tidy glob to run tidy on .go changes`\\n  - `feat(builtins): add shellcheck fix via git apply`\\n  - `feat(builtins): add ls_lint linter`\\n- **Suggested independence:** Proposals 1 and 2 are tiny and low-risk; Proposal 3 is a new tool + stub + tests. They can land in any order.\\n\\n---\\n\\n*AI-assisted — Tool: Claude Code; model: anthropic/claude-opus-4-8[1m]; version: 2.1.219.*\\n\",\"comments\":{\"nodes\":[{\"author\":{\"login\":\"sahidvelji\"},\"body\":\"PRs incoming\",\"replies\":{\"nodes\":[]}},{\"author\":{\"login\":\"jdx\"},\"body\":\"Implemented in https://github.com/jdx/hk/pull/1240.\\n\\nI made two adjustments while validating the proposals:\\n\\n- gomod_tidy explicitly stages go.mod and go.sum, since a Go-source-only trigger can cause tidy to modify manifests that are not job files\\n- ShellCheck uses hk native check_diff application first, with a checked fallback that reruns ShellCheck so processing errors and remaining non-auto-fixable findings are not hidden by pipeline exit semantics\\n\\nThe PR also adds the ls_lint builtin and focused integration coverage for Go manifest staging and ShellCheck fixing across both Git backends.\\n\\n*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: unavailable/unavailable; version: unavailable.*\",\"replies\":{\"nodes\":[]}}]}},{\"number\":1220,\"title\":\"Windows: structured argv builtins cannot resolve `node_modules/.bin` shims (oxlint, eslint, ...)\",\"url\":\"https://github.com/jdx/hk/discussions/1220\",\"body\":\"## Summary\\r\\n\\r\\nSince #1194 (\\\"fix(builtins): preserve file argument boundaries\\\"), builtins migrated to structured argv — e.g. `pkl/builtins/ox_lint.pkl`:\\r\\n\\r\\n```pkl\\r\\ncheck = new Config.CommandSpec {\\r\\n  command = new Config.Command { argv = List(\\\"oxlint\\\", \\\"--deny-warnings\\\", \\\"{{files}}\\\") }\\r\\n  effect = \\\"read\\\"\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nOn Windows, these steps fail with \\\"oxlint\\\" (or \\\"eslint\\\", etc.) not found **only when the tool is installed via `node_modules`**. The same steps work on Linux, and work on Windows when the tool is installed globally (e.g. via mise/cargo/scoop, which ship a real `.exe`).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Environment\\r\\n\\r\\n- OS: Windows\\r\\n- hk: since commit a810c3b (#1194, merged)\\r\\n- Affected builtins: any migrated to argv that resolve to a `node_modules/.bin` shim (oxlint, eslint, ...)\\r\\n- Not affected: Linux; Windows with a globally-installed `.exe`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reproduction\\r\\n\\r\\n1. On Windows, in a repo with `oxlint` (or `eslint`) installed as an npm dev dependency (so `node_modules/.bin/oxlint.cmd` exists).\\r\\n2. Run `hk run check` (or trigger the `ox_lint` / `eslint` step).\\r\\n3. The step fails reporting the executable cannot be found.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Root cause\\r\\n\\r\\n#1194 switched ~100 builtins from shell-string commands to structured `Config.Command { argv = [...] }`. The two command forms take different execution paths in `src/step/runner.rs`:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Shell form** (before #1194) renders to a single string and, on Windows with the default `Cmd` shell, runs via `cmd.exe /c <rendered>` (`runner.rs:296`). `cmd.exe` resolves the executable using `PATHEXT` (`.COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD;...`), so the bare name `oxlint` matches `node_modules/.bin/oxlint.cmd`.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Argv form** (after #1194) runs via `CmdLineRunner::new_direct(&argv[0])` (`runner.rs:276`), which calls Rust's `std::process::Command::new(\\\"oxlint\\\")` directly, bypassing `cmd.exe` entirely (see `ensembler/src/cmd.rs`, `new_direct`).\\r\\n\\r\\nPer the Rust std docs for [`Command` on Windows](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Command.html#searching):\\r\\n\\r\\n> For executable files, the `.exe` extension may be omitted. Files with other extensions must include the extension, otherwise they will not be found.\\r\\n\\r\\n`CreateProcessW` (the Win32 API Rust uses) only appends `.exe`; it does **not** consult `PATHEXT`. npm shims under `node_modules/.bin/` are `oxlint` (extensionless shell script) and `oxlint.cmd` — neither is a `.exe`, so `Command::new(\\\"oxlint\\\")` cannot find them.\\r\\n\\r\\nOn Linux, `new_direct` falls back to `execvp`, which searches `PATH` and happily executes the extensionless shim (it has the executable bit), so the same argv form works.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why only `node_modules` installs are affected\\r\\n\\r\\nGlobal installs (mise, cargo, scoop, ...) provide a real `oxlint.exe`, which `CreateProcessW` resolves via the implicit `.exe` append. `node_modules/.bin/` only provides `.cmd`/extensionless shims, which `CreateProcessW` cannot resolve without `PATHEXT`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Relevant code\\r\\n\\r\\n- `pkl/builtins/ox_lint.pkl` — argv form introduced by #1194\\r\\n- `src/step/runner.rs:276` — `RenderedCommand::Argv(argv) => CmdLineRunner::new_direct(&argv[0]).args(&argv[1..])`\\r\\n- `src/step/runner.rs:296` — shell form on Windows: `CmdLineRunner::new_direct(\\\"cmd.exe\\\").arg(\\\"/c\\\").raw_arg(run)`\\r\\n- `ensembler/src/cmd.rs` — `new()` wraps `cmd.exe /c` on Windows; `new_direct()` does not\\r\\n\",\"comments\":{\"nodes\":[{\"author\":{\"login\":\"jdx\"},\"body\":\"Thanks for the detailed report—the diagnosis is correct. I opened #1221 with a fix.\\n\\nThe change resolves structured-argv executables using the effective Windows `PATH` and `PATHEXT`. Real `.exe`/`.com` programs remain on the direct execution path, while resolved `.cmd`/`.bat` shims run through `cmd.exe` with npm-shim-aware escaping so argument boundaries are preserved.\\n\\nI also added a Windows regression test using a `node_modules/.bin/*.cmd` shim and arguments containing spaces, `&`, `%...%`, `*`, and `^`. The Windows build and Pester suite are passing on the PR.\\n\\n*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: openai/gpt-5; version: unavailable.*\",\"replies\":{\"nodes\":[]}}]}}]}}}}"}

For ready-to-go examples with full source code, see cite83†Examples . For API documentation, see cite84†Standard Library .
L107: ## cite64†Comments L108: 
L109: Pkl has three forms of comments:
L110: 
L111: Line comment
L112: 
L113: 
L114: A code comment that starts with a double-slash (`//`) and runs until the end of the line.
L115: 
L116:     `// Single-line comment`
L117: 
L118: Block comment
L119: 
L120: 
L121: A nestable multiline comment, which is typically used to comment out code. Starts with `/*` and ends with `*/`.
L122: 
L123:     `/*
L124:       Multiline
L125:       comment
L126:     */`
L127: 
L128: Doc comment
L129: A user-facing comment attached to a program member. It starts with a triple-slash (`///`) and runs until the end of the line. Doc comments on consecutive lines are merged.
L130: 
L131:     `/// A *bird* superstar.
L132:     /// Unfortunately, extinct.
L133:     dodo: Bird`
L134: 
L135: Doc comments are processed by cite85†Pkldoc , Pkl’s documentation generator. For details on their syntax, see cite86†Doc Comments .
L136: ## cite65†Numbers L137: 
L138: Pkl has two numeric types, cite87†Int and cite88†Float . Their common supertype is cite89†Number .
L139: ### cite90†Integers L140: 
L141: A value of type cite87†Int is a 64-bit signed integer.
L142: 
L143: Integer literals can be written in decimal, hexadecimal, binary, or octal notation:
L144: 
L145:     `num1 = 123
L146:     num2 = 0x012AFF (1)
L147:     num3 = 0b00010111 (2)
L148:     num4 = 0o755 (3)`
L149: 
L150: 1  | decimal: 76543
L151: 2  | decimal: 23
L152: 3  | decimal: 493
L153: Integers can optionally include an underscore as a separator to improve readability. An underscore does not affect the integer’s value.
L154: 
L155:     `num1 = 1_000_000 (1)
L156:     num2 = 0x0134_64DE (2)
L157:     num3 = 0b0001_0111 (3)
L158:     num4 = 0o0134_6475 (4)`
L159: 
L160: 1  | Equivalent to `1000000`
L161: 2  | Equivalent to `0x013464DE`
L162: 3  | Equivalent to `0b00010111`
L163: 4  | Equivalent to `0o01346475`
L164: 
L165: Negative integer literals start with a minus sign, as in `-123`.
L166: Integers support the standard comparison operators:
L167: 
L168:     `comparison1 = 5 == 2
L169:     comparison2 = 5 < 2
L170:     comparison3 = 5 > 2
L171:     comparison4 = 5 <= 2
L172:     comparison5 = 5 >= 2`
L173: 
L174: Integers support the following arithmetic operators:
L175: 
L176:     `num1 = 5 + 2   (1)
L177:     num2 = 5 - 2   (2)
L178:     num3 = 5 * 2   (3)
L179:     num4 = 5 / 2   (4)
L180:     num5 = 5 ~/ 2  (5)
L181:     num6 = 5 % 2   (6)
L182:     num7 = 5 ** 2  (7)`
L183: 1  | addition (result: `7`)
L184: 2  | subtraction (result: `3`)
L185: 3  | multiplication (result: `10`)
L186: 4  | division (result: `2.5`, always `Float`)
L187: 5  | integer division (result: `2`, always `Int`)
L188: 6  | remainder (result: `1`)
L189: 7  | exponentiation (result: `25`)
L190: 
L191: Arithmetic overflows are caught and result in an error.
L192: 
L193: To restrict an integer’s range, use one of the predefined cite91†type aliases or an cite92†isBetween cite93†type constraint :
L194: 
L195:     `clientPort: UInt16
L196:     serverPort: Int(isBetween(0, 1023))`
L197: ### cite94†Floats L198: 
L199: A value of type cite88†Float is a 64-bit cite95†double-precision†en.wikipedia.org floating point number.
L200: 
L201: Float literals use decimal notation. They consist of an integer part, decimal point, fractional part, and exponent part. The integer and exponent parts are optional.
L202: 
L203:     `num1 = .23
L204:     num2 = 1.23
L205:     num3 = 1.23e2 (1)
L206:     num4 = 1.23e-2 (2)`
L207: 
L208: 1  | result: 1.23 * 10^{2}
L209: 2  | result: 1.23 * 10^{-2}
L210: 
L211: Negative float literals start with a minus sign, as in `-1.23`.
L212: The special float values not a number, positive infinity, and negative infinity are written as:
L213: 
L214:     `notANumber = NaN
L215:     positiveInfinity = Infinity
L216:     negativeInfinity = -Infinity`
L217: 
L218: The cite96†NaN and cite97†Infinity properties are defined in the standard library.
L219: 
L220: Floats support the same comparison and arithmetic operators as integers. Float literals with a fractional part of zero can be safely replaced with integer literals. For example, it is safe to write `1.3 * 42` instead of `1.3 * 42.0`.
L221: Floats can also include the same underscore separator as integers. For example, `1_000.4_400` is a float whose value is equivalent to `1000.4400`.
L222: 
L223:  | As integers are more convenient to use than floats with a fractional part of zero, we recommend requiring `x: Number` instead of `x: Float` in type annotations.
L224: 
L225: To restrict a float to a finite value, use the cite98†isFinite cite93†type constraint :
L226: 
L227:     `x: Float(isFinite)`
L228: To restrict a float’s range, use the cite92†isBetween type constraint:
L229: 
L230:     `x: Float(isBetween(0, 10e6))`
L231: ## cite66†Booleans L232: 
L233: A value of type cite99†Boolean is either `true` or `false`.
L234: 
L235: Apart from the standard logical operators, `Boolean` has cite100†xor and cite101†implies methods.
L236: 
L237:     `res1 = true && false (1)
L238:     res2 = true || false (2)
L239:     res3 = !false (3)
L240:     res4 = true.xor(false) (4)
L241:     res5 = true.implies(false) (5)`
L242: 1  | logical conjunction (result: `false`)
L243: 2  | logical disjunction (result: `true`)
L244: 3  | logical negation (result: `true`)
L245: 4  | exclusive disjunction (result: `true`)
L246: 5  | logical implication (result: `false`)
L247: ## cite67†Strings L248: 
L249: A value of type cite102†String is a sequence of Unicode code points.
L250: 
L251: String literals are enclosed in double quotes:
L252: 
L253:     `"Hello, World!"`
L254: 
L255:  | Except for a few minor differences ^{[cite103†1 ]}, String literals have the same syntax and semantics as in Swift 5. Learn one of them, know both of them!
L256: 
L257: Inside a string literal, the following character escape sequences have special meaning:
L258: 
L259:   * `\t` - tab
L260: 
L261:   * `\n` - line feed
L262: 
L263:   * `\r` - carriage return
L264: 
L265:   * `\"` - verbatim quote
L266:   * `\\` - verbatim backslash
L267: 
L268: Unicode escape sequences have the form `\u{<codePoint>}`, where `<codePoint>` is a hexadecimal number between 0 and 10FFFF:
L269: 
L270:     `"\u{26} \u{E9} \u{1F600}" (1)`
L271: 
L272: 1  | result: `"& é 😀"`
L273: 
L274: To concatenate strings, use the `+` (plus) operator, as in `"abc" + "def" + "ghi"`.
L275: ### cite104†String Interpolation L276: 
L277: To embed the result of expression `<expr>` in a string, use `\(<expr>)`:
L278: 
L279:     `name = "Dodo"
L280:     greeting = "Hi, \(name)!" (1)`
L281: 
L282: 1  | result: `"Hi, Dodo!"`
L283: 
L284: Before a result is inserted, it is converted to a string:
L285: 
L286:     `x = 42
L287:     str = "\(x + 2) plus \(x * 2) is \(0x80)" (1)`
L288: 
L289: 1  | result: `"44 plus 84 is 128"`
L290: ### cite105†Multiline Strings L291: 
L292: To write a string that spans multiple lines, use a multiline string literal:
L293: 
L294:     `"""
L295:     Although the Dodo is extinct,
L296:     the species will be remembered.
L297:     """`
L298: 
L299: Multiline string literals are delimited by three double quotes (`"""`). String content and closing delimiter must each start on a new line.
L300: The content of a multiline string starts on the first line after the opening quotes and ends on the last line before the closing quotes. Line breaks are included in the string and normalized to `\n`.
L301: 
L302: The previous multiline string is equivalent to this single-line string. Notice that there is no leading or trailing whitespace.
L303: 
L304:     `"Although the Dodo is extinct,\n the species will be remembered."`
L305: String interpolation, character escape sequences, and Unicode escape sequences work the same as for single-line strings:
L306: 
L307:     `bird = "Dodo"
L308:     message = """
L309:     Although the \(bird) is extinct,
L310:     the species will be remembered.
L311:     """`

content.text:
I think your instinct is right for **general automated config editing**, but this particular update is narrow enough to work.

Pkl can derive values through inheritance, expressions, and imports. After evaluation, you know the resulting value, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you which source expression to edit. A syntax-preserving parser helps retain formatting; it doesn’t resolve that ambiguity. That’s a real cost of using a programmable configuration language. [Pkl language reference](https://pkl-lang.org/main/current/language-reference/index.html)

The Renovate proposal avoids most of that: it finds **literal package URLs and replaces their versions**. It doesn’t need to evaluate or rewrite the surrounding configuration. I’d support that approach, subject to reviewing the implementation—particularly how its line-based matching handles block comments and multiline strings. The reported test coverage alone doesn’t establish that. [Renovate discussion](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/45740)

Where I’d push back on the hk discussion is the implication that **an older Pkl package necessarily means something is wrong**. The executable and schema/builtins are separate dependencies. {"data":{"repository":{"discussion":{"id":"D_kwDONvxy6M4ApDzT","title":"Keeping the hk version in `hk.pkl` and `mise.toml` in sync with Renovate","url":"https://github.com/jdx/hk/discussions/1344","comments":{"nodes":[{"body":"Update: I've taken the alternative I mentioned at the end of the original post and filed it upstream — **[renovatebot/renovate#45740](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/45740)**, proposing a `pkl` manager rather than a preset.

I changed my mind on which route is better for two reasons:

- Managers are enabled by default, so every repo with an `hk.pkl` gets fixed with no configuration at all. A preset here only helps repos that opt in with `"extends": ["github>jdx/hk"]`.
- A manager also emits the same `depName`/`packageName` as Renovate's existing `mise` manager, so `mise.toml` and `hk.pkl` group into one PR automatically, without the `packageRules` entry the preset needed.

It's implemented and ready — extraction covers `amends`, `extends` and `import` clauses plus `import` expressions, mapped onto the existing `github-releases` datasource with no new datasource required, verified against real `hk.pkl` files. I'm waiting on a maintainer to weigh in before raising the PR.

So I'd suggest holding on question 1 in the original post. If the manager lands, the preset here isn't needed; if it's declined, the preset proposal stands as written and I'm still happy to write it.

Question 2 is unaffected either way: `hk = "latest"` can't be managed by Renovate regardless of which route wins, since `semver-coerced` rejects `latest` and the dependency is skipped. Pinning is what makes the tool side manageable at all.
"}]}}}}}
